Sessions begin on 1 October, but people can register their interest at any time.

When asked why she believed black and marginalised girls and women may be deterred from playing football, Csillag said: “The most important part is a lack of role models. Maybe also not being able to access it.

“They [also might be] struggling with their confidence. For example, I was so different when I started to play football and my body was so different. I played in a team where the whole team were white girls and our body structure was so different and I lost some confidence.

“I said: ‘Why am I so tall? Why are my thighs so big? Why is this different?’ I just started to compare myself with them and maybe a lot of other girls may have lost their confidence. They may not keep going because of a lack of support or awareness.

“If I had one [other black person on the team] they would know what I was talking about. That is why I am so happy that in the national team we have four black girls and five years ago it was only one or two. For Csillag, it starts at the top. “The most important thing is that you have black people in the staff, higher up, because I barely see this,” she says. “Every time I see it I think: ‘Woah, I could one day maybe reach what she is reaching.’
“When you have never seen it, how can a little girl think she can do it? It will go automatically that young girls will follow that dream or path. Visibility starts at the top.”
